---
title: "Lab 10: Multiple Linear Regression II"
---

## Packages for Today (Install if Needed)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(ppcor)
library(car)
library(gridExtra)
```
:::


## Overview

Functions: 

* `ppcor::pcor(data)`: partial correlation
* `ppcor::spcor(data)`: semi-partial correlation
* `car::vif(lm_output)`: variance inflation factor
* `hatvalues(lm_output)`: leverage
* `residuals(lm_output)`: model residuals
* `rstandard(lm_output)`: internally studentized residuals (distance measure)
* `rstudent(lm_output)`: externally studentized residuals (preferred distance measure)
* `dffits(lm_output)`: DFFITS influence measure
* `dfbetas(lm_output)`: DFBETAS influence measure
* `cooks.distance(lm_output)`: Cook's distance influence measure
* `covratio(lm_output)`: COVRATIO influence measure



## Data

We'll work with the States data again today. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat <- read_xlsx("States.xlsx", sheet = 1)
```
:::


Last week, we predicted the number of airports from total square miles and population. We found that our variables are somewhat more normally distributed with fewer outliers if we take logs of each variable.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat <- dat %>% 
  mutate(logNairports = log(Nairports),
         logTotalSqMiles = log(TotalSqMiles),
         logPopulation = log(Population))
```
:::


## Types of Correlations

There are three types of correlations that we can look at for these data. 

* Ordinary bivariate Pearson correlations
* Partial correlations
* Semipartial correlations

## Bivariate Pearson Correlations


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pears_cor <- cor(dat[, c("logNairports", 
                         "logTotalSqMiles", 
                         "logPopulation")])
pears_cor
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                logNairports logTotalSqMiles logPopulation
logNairports       1.0000000       0.7141517     0.5216795
logTotalSqMiles    0.7141517       1.0000000     0.2092757
logPopulation      0.5216795       0.2092757     1.0000000
```


:::
:::


These pairwise correlations ignore the existence of the other variable.

## Partial Correlations

Partial and semi-partial correlations can be computed in R using the `ppcor` package. The function `pcor()` function calculates partial correlations, and the function `spcor()` function calculates semi-partial correlations. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
partial_cor <- pcor(dat[, c("logNairports", 
                            "logTotalSqMiles", 
                            "logPopulation")])
partial_cor$estimate
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                logNairports logTotalSqMiles logPopulation
logNairports       1.0000000       0.7251744     0.5437983
logTotalSqMiles    0.7251744       1.0000000    -0.2734176
logPopulation      0.5437983      -0.2734176     1.0000000
```


:::
:::




Partial correlations are at the intersection of the two variables of interest, other variables are partialled out. These reflect the shared variance between the two variables that is not shared by the other variables.

## Semi-partial Correlations


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
semipartial_cor <- spcor(dat[, c("logNairports", 
                                 "logTotalSqMiles", 
                                 "logPopulation")])
semipartial_cor$estimate
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                logNairports logTotalSqMiles logPopulation
logNairports       1.0000000       0.6186764     0.3806539
logTotalSqMiles    0.7091166       1.0000000    -0.1913898
logPopulation      0.5317568      -0.2332639     1.0000000
```


:::
:::


Semi-partial correlations are not symmetric. Look for the DV in the rows, and the IV of interest in the columns. For example, $0.6186764^2 = 0.3827605$ is the proportion of variance in `logNairports` that is uniquely predicted by `logTotalSqMiles`, above and beyond `logPopulation`.

## Comparing Three Types of Correlations

Considering the three types of correlations, treating `logNairports` as the DV.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pears_cor[1, 2:3]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
logTotalSqMiles   logPopulation 
      0.7141517       0.5216795 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
partial_cor$estimate[1, 2:3]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
logTotalSqMiles   logPopulation 
      0.7251744       0.5437983 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
semipartial_cor$estimate[1, 2:3]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
logTotalSqMiles   logPopulation 
      0.6186764       0.3806539 
```


:::
:::


## Comparing Three Types of Correlations

Partial correlations are always larger in magnitude than semi-partial correlations. There is no necessary relationships between these and the bivariate Pearson correlation. In fact, if there are distorting effects, the Pearson correlations can have a different sign than the partial or semi-partial correlations!


## Variance Inflation Factor

At this point, we'll add the two-digit state abbreviation as row names to the dataset. Although the tidyverse doesn't particularly like the use of row names, these will help us make sense of our regression diagnostics later.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat <- dat %>%
  column_to_rownames("Abbreviation")
```
:::


We will next fit the regression model (without taking logs) from last week.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod1 <- lm(Nairports ~ TotalSqMiles + Population, dat)
vif(mod1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
TotalSqMiles   Population 
    1.017082     1.017082 
```


:::
:::


In this example, the VIF is very close to 1 for both predictors, meaning that the standard errors of the associated regression coefficients is minimally affected by the presence of other predictors. 

## Variance Inflation Factor

As a second example, suppose we think incarceration rates are related to religious and political views.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod2 <- lm(IncarcerationRate2018 ~ PctIrreligion + 
             PctHarris2024 + PctTrump2024, dat)
summary(mod2)$coefficients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                 Estimate Std. Error    t value  Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   -2801.40283 2943.00473 -0.9518853 0.3461302
PctIrreligion    -6.96092    4.75179 -1.4649049 0.1497486
PctHarris2024    40.34467   29.51451  1.3669436 0.1782866
PctTrump2024     31.25470   29.56891  1.0570123 0.2960256
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
vif(mod2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
PctIrreligion PctHarris2024  PctTrump2024 
     1.700883    206.830480    198.217952 
```


:::
:::


## Variance Inflation Factor

(Because the U.S. doesn't have robust third parties), `PctHarris2024` and `PctTrump2024` are highly (negatively) correlated. As a result, we don't gain much predictive power from including both, and we lose a lot in terms of power, as reflected by the increased standard errors of the estimated coefficients.

`mod2` has moderate predictive power. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(mod2)$r.squared
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.4624605
```


:::
:::


This is also a good place to remind ourselves that correlation does not equal causation. Even if we can predict a phenomenon fairly well, that does not mean that we have identified the causes of the DV.


## Evaluating Model Residuals

For the hypothesis tests to be accurate, we need to satisfy certain assumptions about the residuals:

* Normality
* Homoscedasticity

Heteroscedasticity of residuals can suggest an omitted variable or an omitted curvilinear relationship between a predictor and the outcome.

## Evaluating Model Residuals

To analyze residuals graphically, it is convenient to add model residuals to the data. Here, we return to predicting airports.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod1b <- lm(logNairports ~ logTotalSqMiles + logPopulation, dat)
dat2 <- dat %>% mutate(residuals = residuals(mod1b))
```
:::


## Evaluating Model Residuals

To evaluate homoscedasticity, we can plot the residuals against each predictor. Adding a loess line with standard error bar to this plot can help us interpret the results. We want to look for:

* Whether the residuals are centered at the 0 line.
* Whether the residuals are evenly distributed across all levels of each predictor.

Plots on the next slide.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot1 <- ggplot(dat2, aes(logTotalSqMiles, residuals)) + geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = loess, se = TRUE, formula = y ~ x) + 
  scale_x_log10() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
plot2 <- ggplot(dat2, aes(logPopulation, residuals)) + geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = loess, se = TRUE, formula = y ~ x) + 
  scale_x_log10() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
gridExtra::grid.arrange(plot1, plot2, nrow = 1)
```
:::


## Evaluating Model Residuals



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Multiple_Linear_Regression_II_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


For both variables, positive and negative residuals have about the same magnitudes. Heteroscedasticity is harder to ascertain because there are relatively few data points, but there are no major signs of concern (the quadratic-like relationship for `logPopulation` may be related to the limitations of a linear model) 

## Evaluating Model Residuals

We can also evaluate the normality of residuals using our usual methods such as qq plots. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(dat2, aes(sample = residuals)) + 
  geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Multiple_Linear_Regression_II_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


There is some deviation from normality, possibly caused by the remaining outliers in the data (which we will evaluate next).

## Leverage

For leverage values, we want to take a closer look at values greater than $3(p+1) / N = 9 / 50 = .18$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
leverage <- hatvalues(mod1b)
```
:::


It can be difficult to visually identify individual values. Instead, we pick out leverage values greater than the cutoff for each model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
leverage[leverage > .18]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       AK        RI 
0.2379028 0.2214389 
```


:::
:::


In `mod1`, Alaska and Rhode Island (the states with the highest and lowest total square miles) have the highest leverage.

## Distance

Distance measures consider unusual values of the criterion given the predictors. 

For externally studentized residuals, we want to take a closer look at values greater than 2.5. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distance <- rstudent(mod1b)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distance[distance > 2.5]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      AK       HI       RI 
2.642931 2.573633 2.802997 
```


:::
:::


Here, the first model identifiesAlaska, Hawaii, and Rhode Island as possible outliers. 

## Influence

Leverage and distance are useful for telling which observations are unusual relative to the other observations. Neither of these statistics necessarily means that the observation has high impact. 

Influence measures are most useful for this purpose:

* DFFITS
* DFBETAS
* Cook's Distance
* COVRATIO

## Influence

Let's look at DFFITS first, which looks at the standardized change in predicted scores. We want to flag observations higher than $2\sqrt{(p+1)/N} = 2\sqrt{.06} = .49$ for large sample sizes, and higher than 1 for moderate sample sizes. I consider 50 to be closer to "moderate" than "large", but let's explore both cutoffs. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dffits_mod1 <- dffits(mod1b)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dffits_mod1[abs(dffits_mod1) > .49]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       AK        FL        HI        RI 
1.4766596 0.5071895 0.6859681 1.4948694 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dffits_mod1[abs(dffits_mod1) > 1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      AK       RI 
1.476660 1.494869 
```


:::
:::


Again, we flag Alaska (high area state), Florida (high area and high population states), Rhode Island (low area state), and Hawaii (relatively low area, but more reliant on air travel). 

## Influence

Next, let's look at DFBETAS, which looks at the standardized change in regression coefficients. We want to flag observations with absolute values higher than $2/\sqrt{N} = 2/\sqrt{50} = .28$ for large samples, and > 1 for moderate samples. This measure considers each regression coefficient separately. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dfbetas_mod1 <- dfbetas(mod1b)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dfbetas_mod1[apply(abs(dfbetas_mod1[, 2:3]) > .28, 1, any), ]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   (Intercept) logTotalSqMiles logPopulation
AK   0.1834033     1.214172987    -0.9612674
FL  -0.3744598    -0.008871632     0.4256553
HI   0.5459502    -0.427899479    -0.2835408
NY  -0.2832973    -0.042352743     0.3465093
RI   1.0911211    -1.302380106    -0.2947791
VT  -0.4036340     0.202353219     0.2899512
WY   0.2646751     0.214444384    -0.4118267
```


:::
:::


States with extreme physical area or populations are identified as influential for either slope coefficients. Alaska, Hawaii, and Rhode Island are only states to have high influence on TotSqMiles.

## Influence

Next, let's apply Cook's distance, which looks at the standardized *squared* difference in predicted scores. Here, we use a cutoff of 1. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cook <- cooks.distance(mod1b)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cook[cook > 1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
named numeric(0)
```


:::
:::


No states have high distance.

## Influence

Finally, let's look at COVRATIO, which looks at the change in the standard errors of regression coefficients. Here, we use a cutoff of |COVRATIO-1| $\geq 3p/N$, and because our COVRATIO values are positive, this translates to a cutoff of 1.12. Similar high-area and small-area states are again identified.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covratio_mod1 <- covratio(mod1b)
covratio_mod1[covratio_mod1 > 1.12]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      CA       CT       DE       MA       MT       NH       NJ       SD 
1.180613 1.158783 1.293882 1.126728 1.158153 1.139910 1.137924 1.156046 
      TX 
1.141941 
```


:::
:::


## Summary

This is a tricky example case. Alaska, in particular, seems to be the most influential point. Alaska is indeed unusual in that it has a relatively small population, but it is easily the largest U.S. state and it has a large number of airports (because air travel is either the most convenient, or the only, way to arrive at many Alaskan towns). Other states with relatively large populations, including California, Texas, New York, and Florida, and small areas, including Rhode Island and Hawaii, also seem to have outsized influence, so it may be worthwhile to continue exploring nonlinear transformations of the predictors. 

To improve this model, we might try to identify variables to add to the model that would better reflect the reasons why Alaska is unusual. Another option we could try for modeling these data is to assume a nonlinear relationship between the number of airports and the inputted variables. More advanced generalized linear models (GLMs) such as poisson regression or negative binomial regression (not covered in detail in this course) may be more appropriate, especially because Nairports is a count variable.
